[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Schema Evolution, Versioning, and Deprecation in GraphQL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike traditional REST APIs that often rely on URL versioning (such as /api/v1/users), GraphQL APIs are designed around a single evolving endpoint. Schema evolution in GraphQL focuses on additive changes, allowing you to update your data graph without breaking existing clients."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The GraphQL Philosophy: Avoid Versioning"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In a well-designed GraphQL schema, breaking changes should be exceptionally rare. Because clients explicitly request only the fields they need, adding new types, fields, or arguments does not impact legacy queries. This enables continuous deployment of your backend schema."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Deprecating Fields Using the @deprecated Directive"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you need to restructure your data, you should never delete a field that clients might still be using. Instead, mark the old field as deprecated using the built-in @deprecated directive. This informs consumers that the field will be removed in a future release and provides a clear migration path."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"type User {
  id: ID!
  # Old field, scheduled for removal
  fullName: String @deprecated(reason: "Use firstName and lastName instead.")
  firstName: String
  lastName: String
}"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Schema Evolution"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always add new fields instead of modifying existing ones whenever possible."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Provide descriptive reasons inside the @deprecated directive to guide client developers."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor field usage via telemetry and query logs before finally removing deprecated fields."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Handling True Breaking Changes"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"If a breaking change is strictly unavoidable (such as a foundational type restructuring), you must treat it like releasing a new major version of an API. This involves deploying a parallel schema, notifying consumers, and eventually decommissioning the old endpoint or namespace."}]
